claim: Eukaryotic mismatch repair (MMR) utilizes single-strand breaks as signals to target the strand to be repaired.
source: Eukaryotic mismatch repair (MMR) utilizes single-strand breaks as signals to target the strand to be repaired.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about eukaryotic MMR.

claim: DNA-bound PCNA is presumed to direct MMR.
source: DNA-bound PCNA is also presumed to direct MMR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a presumption in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: DNA-bound PCNA induces strand-specific MMR in the absence of strand discontinuities.
source: We show that DNA-bound PCNA induces strand-specific MMR in the absence of strand discontinuities.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: MutSα inhibited PCNA unloading through its PCNA-interacting motif.
source: Strikingly, MutSα inhibited PCNA unloading through its PCNA-interacting motif, thereby extending significantly the temporal window permissive to strand-specific MMR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 6, 8, and 9.

claim: MutSα extends the temporal window permissive to strand-specific MMR.
source: Strikingly, MutSα inhibited PCNA unloading through its PCNA-interacting motif, thereby extending significantly the temporal window permissive to strand-specific MMR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing extended half-life of strand memory in the presence of MutSα.

claim: MMR increases replication fidelity by ~2 orders of magnitude in yeast.
source: By rectifying replication errors, MMR increases the replication fidelity by ~2 orders of magnitude in yeast (Lujan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lujan et al., 2014.

claim: Genetic or epigenetic inactivation of MMR genes elevates the risk of tumorigenesis in humans.
source: In humans, genetic or epigenetic inactivation of MMR genes elevates the risk of tumorigenesis in both hereditary and sporadic manners (Jiricny, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiricny, 2013.

claim: In E. coli, MMR distinguishes parental and daughter strands mainly by using adenine methylation on GATC sites.
source: In Escherichia coli, MMR distinguishes the parental and daughter strands mainly by using adenine methylation on GATC sites (Lahue et al., 1989; Iyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lahue et al., 1989 and Iyer et al., 2006.

claim: Over-expression of Dam methylase significantly elevates mutation frequency in E. coli.
source: Maintaining this temporal window is critical for efficient MMR, because over-expression of the Dam methylase, by which full-methylation of the GATC sites is accelerated, significantly elevates the mutation frequency (Herman and Modrich, 1981; Marinus et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herman and Modrich, 1981 and Marinus et al., 1984.

claim: E. coli MMR can correct replication errors through a methylation-independent mechanism using strand discontinuities.
source: The E. coli MMR system can also correct replication errors through a methylation-independent mechanism, where strand discontinuities can substitute for GATC methylation both in vivo and in vitro (Laengle-Rouault et al., 1986; Lahue et al., 1987; 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laengle-Rouault et al., 1986 and Lahue et al., 1987; 1989.

claim: Eukaryotic MMR is directed by strand discontinuities such as nicks or gaps in vitro.
source: Eukaryotic MMR is directed by strand discontinuities such as nicks or gaps in vitro (Holmes et al., 1990; Thomas et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmes et al., 1990 and Thomas et al., 1991.

claim: MutSα has a biased preference for base-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops.
source: MutSα has a biased preference for base-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops (IDLs), while MutSβ preferentially recognizes large IDLs (Iyer et al., 2006; Jiricny, 2013; Kunkel and Erie, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iyer et al., 2006; Jiricny, 2013; and Kunkel and Erie, 2015.

claim: MutSβ preferentially recognizes large insertion/deletion loops.
source: MutSα has a biased preference for base-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops (IDLs), while MutSβ preferentially recognizes large IDLs (Iyer et al., 2006; Jiricny, 2013; Kunkel and Erie, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iyer et al., 2006; Jiricny, 2013; and Kunkel and Erie, 2015.

claim: Single-strand DNA termini such as 5'-ends of Okazaki fragments serve as entry points for Exo1 and strand discrimination signals in vivo.
source: Single-strand DNA termini such as 5'-ends of the Okazaki fragments serve as entry points for Exo1 and strand discrimination signals in vivo as well (Pavlov et al., 2003; Nick McElhinny et al., 2010; Liberti et al., 2013; Lujan et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pavlov et al., 2003; Nick McElhinny et al., 2010; Liberti et al., 2013; Lujan et al., 2014; and Liu et al., 2015.

claim: Ribonucleotides embedded by replicative DNA polymerases serve as strand signals for MMR in vitro.
source: Recent studies have revealed that ribonucleotides embedded by replicative DNA polymerases serve as strand signals for MMR in vitro and contribute to a sub-fraction of leading strand MMR in vivo, after converted into single-strand gaps through RNaseH2-dependent ribonucleotide excision repair (Ghodgaonkar et al., 2013; Lujan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ghodgaonkar et al., 2013 and Lujan et al., 2013.

claim: PCNA is loaded onto DNA from the template-primer junction by RFC.
source: PCNA is loaded onto DNA from the template-primer junction by RFC, and likely unloaded by an RFC-like complex containing Elg1 after the completion of DNA synthesis (Kubota et al., 2013; 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kubota et al., 2013 and 2015.

claim: PCNA is likely unloaded by an RFC-like complex containing Elg1 after the completion of DNA synthesis.
source: PCNA is loaded onto DNA from the template-primer junction by RFC, and likely unloaded by an RFC-like complex containing Elg1 after the completion of DNA synthesis (Kubota et al., 2013; 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kubota et al., 2013 and 2015.

claim: PCNA's DNA binding is asymmetric with respect to polarities of the parental and daughter strands.
source: Since its DNA binding is asymmetric with respect to polarities of the parental and daughter strands, DNA-bound PCNA can hold information for the newly synthesized strand (Bowman et al., 2004; Georgescu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowman et al., 2004 and Georgescu et al., 2015.

claim: PCNA plays an essential role in an early MMR step that precedes degradation of the error-carrying strand.
source: PCNA plays an essential role in an early MMR step that precedes degradation of the error-carrying strand (Umar et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Umar et al., 1996.

claim: PCNA loaded from a strand discontinuity induces strand-specific, mismatch- and MutSα-dependent activation of the MutLα endonuclease.
source: PCNA loaded from a strand discontinuity induces strand-specific, mismatch- and MutSα-dependent activation of the MutLα endonuclease (Kadyrov et al., 2006; 2007; Pluciennik et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kadyrov et al., 2006; 2007; and Pluciennik et al., 2010.

claim: When PCNA is loaded onto closed circular DNA without defined orientation, it induces unbiased nicking on both DNA strands.
source: When PCNA is loaded onto closed circular DNA without defined orientation, it induces unbiased nicking on both DNA strands (Pluciennik et al., 2010; 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pluciennik et al., 2010 and 2013.

claim: Numbers of PCNA mutants in yeast exhibit mutator phenotypes that are epistatic to MMR mutations.
source: Numbers of PCNA mutants in yeast exhibit mutator phenotypes that are epistatic to MMR mutations (Johnson et al., 1996; Umar et al., 1996; Chen et al., 1999; Amin et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2002; Goellner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 1996; Umar et al., 1996; Chen et al., 1999; Amin et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2002; and Goellner et al., 2014.

claim: PCNA interacts with MutSα/β through their PCNA-interacting peptide (PIP) motifs.
source: It interacts with MutSα/β through their PCNA-interacting peptide (PIP) motifs, which reside at the N-termini of Msh6 and Msh3 (Clark et al., 2000; Flores-Rozas et al., 2000; Kleczkowska et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2000; Flores-Rozas et al., 2000; and Kleczkowska et al., 2001.

claim: The PIP motifs in Msh6 and Msh3 are connected to the mispair binding domains through long linkers predicted to be disordered in yeast.
source: In both cases, the PIP motifs and the mispair binding domains are connected through long linkers, which are predicted to be disordered in yeast (Shell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shell et al., 2007.

claim: Mutants of the PIP motifs in Msh6 and Msh3 show substantial but not complete reduction of MMR activity.
source: Mutants of the PIP motifs in Msh6 and Msh3 show substantial but not complete reduction of the MMR activity, indicating that the PIP motif plays an important, yet assistive, non-essential role in MMR (Clark et al., 2000; Flores-Rozas et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark et al., 2000 and Flores-Rozas et al., 2000.

claim: The PIP motif has been proposed to tether MutSα to the replication fork to assist its mismatch recognition.
source: The PIP motif has been proposed to tether MutSα to the replication fork to assist its mismatch recognition (Kleczkowska et al., 2001; Hombauer et al., 2011a; Haye and Gammie, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kleczkowska et al., 2001; Hombauer et al., 2011a; and Haye and Gammie, 2015.

claim: The PIP motif in MutSα is important for a late MMR step involving degradation of the error-carrying strand, especially by the Exo1-independent mechanism.
source: A recent study has shown that this motif in MutSα is important for a late MMR step(s) involving degradation of the error-carrying strand, especially by the Exo1-independent mechanism (Goellner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goellner et al., 2014.

claim: In yeast, MutSα must be present during S-phase to suppress mutations.
source: It has been shown in yeast that MutSα must be present during S-phase to suppress mutations (Hombauer et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hombauer et al., 2011b.

claim: NPE efficiently promotes gap-directed, strand-specific MMR.
source: These results demonstrate that NPE efficiently recapitulates gap-directed, bi-directional MMR that is dependent on both MutSα/β and MutLα/β/γ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Gap-directed MMR in NPE is dependent on both MutSα/β and MutLα/β/γ.
source: These results demonstrate that NPE efficiently recapitulates gap-directed, bi-directional MMR that is dependent on both MutSα/β and MutLα/β/γ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E showing abolishment of repair upon depletion of these complexes.

claim: NPE supports bidirectional MMR.
source: As seen previously (Olivera Harris et al., 2015), a gap could be placed on either 5' or 3' of the mismatch, and repair DNA synthesis occurred preferentially within a fragment containing the shorter path between the gap and the mismatch (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that NPE supports bidirectional MMR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A nick did not efficiently induce MMR in NPE.
source: Unlike other systems, a nick did not efficiently induce MMR (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Gap-directed A to G MMR was more efficient in NPE (67%) than in HSS (34%).
source: Gap-directed A to G MMR was more efficient in NPE (67%) than in HSS (34%), indicating that NPE has higher MMR activity than HSS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNA synthesis at the gap site was mostly completed within 30 s in NPE.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, DNA synthesis at the gap site (estimated by digestion with PacI placed within the gap) was mostly completed within 30 s.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A to G MMR gradually progressed until ~30 min in NPE.
source: The A to G MMR gradually progressed until ~30 min, and shortly after the mismatch correction, closed circular molecules were accumulated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Efficient DNA synthesis at the gap site precedes mismatch correction involving degradation of the error-carrying strand in NPE.
source: These observations suggest that, in this gap-directed MMR model, efficient DNA synthesis at the gap site precedes mismatch correction involving degradation of the error-carrying strand.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The strand information derived from a gap is 'memorized' on DNA to induce subsequent MMR.
source: These data suggest that the strand information derived from a gap is 'memorized' on DNA to induce subsequent MMR.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2 where MMR efficiency exceeded the amount of remaining strand discontinuities.

claim: More than 80% of gap-carrying plasmids were converted into the closed-circular form within 1.5 min in MutS-depleted NPE.
source: In the MutS-depleted NPE, more than 80% of gap-carrying plasmids were converted into the closed-circular form within 1.5 min (Figure 2B, lane 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ~40% of A to G MMR was still observed upon addition of fresh NPE at 2 min, when at most only ~14% strand discontinuities remained.
source: However, ~40% of A to G MMR was still observed upon addition of fresh NPE at 2 min, at a time when at most, only ~14% strand discontinuities remained (Figure 2B, lane 10 and Figure 2C, lane 14).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The gap-filling reaction in Xenopus egg extracts was PCNA-dependent.
source: The gap-filling reaction in Xenopus egg extracts was PCNA-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4-10 hPCNA trimers reproducibly loaded on DNA in a nick- and ATP-dependent manner.
source: Using fluorescent-based quantitative western blotting, we estimated that 4–10 hPCNA trimers reproducibly loaded on the DNA in a nick- and ATP-dependent manner (Figure 3B; see also Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4.

claim: Ligation of the nick was ~80% efficient in the in vitro PCNA-loading reaction.
source: Ligation of the nick was ~80% efficient.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the in vitro PCNA-loading assay.

claim: DNA-bound hPCNA topologically encircled DNA with free-sliding ability.
source: The DNA-bound hPCNA topologically encircled DNA with free-sliding ability, because linearization of DNA resulted in dissociation of essentially all hPCNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ~75% of the A bases were specifically repaired into G bases when the hPCNA-DNA complex was transferred into NPE.
source: When the hPCNA-DNA complex was transferred into NPE, ~75% of the A bases were specifically repaired into G bases (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The hPCNA-DNA complex prepared with A-nick DNA directed ~60% of A to G MMR.
source: Critically, the hPCNA-DNA complex prepared with A-nick DNA directed ~60% of A to G MMR, and the complex prepared with C-nick DNA directed ~70% of C to T MMR in NPE (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The hPCNA-DNA complex prepared with C-nick DNA directed ~70% of C to T MMR.
source: Critically, the hPCNA-DNA complex prepared with A-nick DNA directed ~60% of A to G MMR, and the complex prepared with C-nick DNA directed ~70% of C to T MMR in NPE (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: When either PCNA or RFC was omitted from the reaction, most of the strand-specific repair was inhibited.
source: When either PCNA or RFC was omitted from the reaction, most of the strand-specific repair was inhibited (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PCNA-directed MMR reaction was dependent on both MutSα/β and MutLα/β/γ.
source: The PCNA-directed MMR reaction was dependent on both MutSα/β and MutLα/β/γ (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Directional loading of hPCNA is sufficient to induce strand-specific MMR in the absence of strand discontinuities in NPE.
source: These results indicate that directional loading of hPCNA is sufficient to induce strand-specific MMR in the absence of strand discontinuities in NPE.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing strand-specific MMR with directionally loaded PCNA.

claim: A significant portion of nick ligation was independent of PCNA.
source: Consistent with this idea, a significant portion of nick ligation was independent of PCNA, explaining why a nick did not induce MMR as efficiently as a gap in NPE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCNA is removed from DNA mostly through an active unloading process requiring the Rfc3-containing complex(es).
source: In the mock-treated NPE, hPCNA was quickly dissociated from a homoduplex DNA within a few minutes, while dissociation was attenuated in the NPE depleted of xRfc3, indicating that PCNA is removed from DNA mostly through an active unloading process requiring the Rfc3-containing complex(es) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the MutS-depleted NPE, hPCNA was quickly unloaded from mismatch-carrying DNA.
source: In the MutS-depleted NPE, hPCNA was again quickly unloaded from mismatch-carrying DNA (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Concurrent with PCNA unloading in MutS-depleted NPE, the PCNA-directed MMR capability rapidly dropped, leaving only ~10% of repairable molecules at 5 min.
source: Concurrent with PCNA unloading, the PCNA-directed MMR capability rapidly dropped, leaving only ~10% of repairable molecules at 5 min (Figure 6C, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the MutL-depleted NPE, even at 30 min, more than one hPCNA trimer on an average still remained on DNA.
source: In contrast, in the MutL-depleted NPE (containing endogenous MutSα/β but deficient for MMR), even at 30 min, more than one hPCNA trimer on an average still remained on DNA, and ~20% of mismatches were still repairable (Figure 6C, lane 14).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the MutL-depleted NPE, ~20% of mismatches were still repairable at 30 min.
source: In contrast, in the MutL-depleted NPE (containing endogenous MutSα/β but deficient for MMR), even at 30 min, more than one hPCNA trimer on an average still remained on DNA, and ~20% of mismatches were still repairable (Figure 6C, lane 14).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mismatch-bound MutS complexes interfere with unloading of PCNA to retain strand information for MMR.
source: These results suggest that mismatch-bound MutS complexes interfere with unloading of PCNA to retain strand information for MMR.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing differential PCNA retention in the presence and absence of MutS.

claim: In either MutS-depleted or MutS/MutL-depleted NPE, more than 40% of mismatches were still repairable upon addition of fresh NPE at 2 min.
source: In either MutS-depleted or MutS/MutL-depleted NPE, more than 40% of mismatches were still repairable upon addition of fresh NPE at 2 min, confirming the ~2 min strand memory seen in Figure 2 (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: In the MutL-depleted NPE, >60% of mismatches were repairable at 10 min.
source: Strikingly, in the MutL-depleted NPE, >60% of mismatches were repairable at 10 min, and ~35% were still repairable even at 30 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: In the MutL-depleted NPE, ~35% of mismatches were still repairable even at 30 min.
source: Strikingly, in the MutL-depleted NPE, >60% of mismatches were repairable at 10 min, and ~35% were still repairable even at 30 min.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The half-life of the strand memory in the absence of MutSα/β is approximately 2 min.
source: Using one-phase exponential decay fitting, which could explain most data with reasonable quality (R2 > 0.8), we estimated the half-life of the strand memory in the absence of MutSα/β to be approximately 2 min, and to be approximately 40 min in the presence of MutSα/β (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The half-life of the strand memory in the presence of MutSα/β is approximately 40 min.
source: Using one-phase exponential decay fitting, which could explain most data with reasonable quality (R2 > 0.8), we estimated the half-life of the strand memory in the absence of MutSα/β to be approximately 2 min, and to be approximately 40 min in the presence of MutSα/β (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The MutSα/β-dependent mechanism maintains the strand information by inhibiting unloading of PCNA that is loaded during DNA synthesis at the gap site.
source: These results strongly suggest that the MutSα/β-dependent mechanism maintains the strand information by inhibiting unloading of PCNA that is loaded during DNA synthesis at the gap site.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing extended strand memory in the presence of MutSα/β.

claim: xMutSαPIP was largely restored for gap-directed MMR in MutS-depleted NPE.
source: In good agreement with previous reports (Kleczkowska et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2008; Bowen et al., 2013), when no stepwise incubation was involved, the gap-directed MMR on the 3.0 kb substrate was largely restored by xMutSαPIP in MutS-depleted NPE (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating that in this experimental setup the PIP function is not important for MMR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mismatch binding of xMutSαPIP was not significantly compromised.
source: Mismatch binding of xMutSαPIP was not significantly compromised (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: xMutSαPIP was almost inert for PCNA retention.
source: However, xMutSαPIP was almost inert for PCNA retention.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: xMutSαWT attenuated PCNA unloading.
source: Although xMutSαWT attenuated PCNA unloading, xMutSαPIP did not exhibit detectable retention of PCNA on mismatched DNA, compared to the buffer control (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: xMutSαPIP did not exhibit detectable retention of PCNA on mismatched DNA, compared to the buffer control.
source: Although xMutSαWT attenuated PCNA unloading, xMutSαPIP did not exhibit detectable retention of PCNA on mismatched DNA, compared to the buffer control (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: xMutSαWT restored retention of strand memory in the MutS/MutL-depleted NPE with a half-life of 25.5 min.
source: In the gap-derived strand memory assay, xMutSαWT restored retention of strand memory in the MutS/MutL-depleted NPE without affecting the gap-filling reaction (t1/2 = 25.5 min; Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1, and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 and Table 2.

claim: xMutSαPIP showed only modest restoration of the retention of strand information with a half-life of 12.5 min.
source: In contrast, only modest restoration of the retention of strand information was seen with xMutSαPIP (t1/2 = 12.5 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 and Table 2.

claim: The PIP motif is required for inhibition of PCNA unloading and largely responsible for strand memory retention.
source: These results indicate that the PIP motif is required for inhibition of PCNA unloading and largely responsible for strand memory retention, yet a PIP-independent mechanism also contributes to the retention of strand information derived from a gap.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing xMutSαWT and xMutSαPIP.

claim: A PIP-independent mechanism also contributes to the retention of strand information derived from a gap.
source: These results indicate that the PIP motif is required for inhibition of PCNA unloading and largely responsible for strand memory retention, yet a PIP-independent mechanism also contributes to the retention of strand information derived from a gap.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing partial strand memory retention by xMutSαPIP and xMutSαΔN.

claim: xMutSαΔN was essentially deficient in PCNA retention.
source: As with xMutSαPIP, xMutSαΔN did not show significant defects in gap-directed MMR and in mismatch binding (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and was essentially deficient in PCNA retention (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The xMutSαΔN complex partially restored the strand memory reaction, with an estimated half-life of 12.3 min.
source: Interestingly, the xMutSαΔN complex partially restored the strand memory reaction, with an estimated half-life of 12.3 min, although it did not affect the kinetics of the sealing of the gap in the first NPE (Figure 9 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 and Table 2.

claim: The retention of strand memory is mediated largely by the PIP motif in MutSα.
source: We concluded that the retention of strand memory is mediated largely by the PIP motif in MutSα, and there is a partial strand memory retention that is independent of the NTR of Msh6.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data comparing different MutSα mutants.

claim: There is a partial strand memory retention that is independent of the NTR of Msh6.
source: We concluded that the retention of strand memory is mediated largely by the PIP motif in MutSα, and there is a partial strand memory retention that is independent of the NTR of Msh6.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing partial strand memory retention by xMutSαΔN.

claim: PCNA transiently remains on DNA after the completion of DNA synthesis.
source: Since PCNA transiently remains on DNA after the completion of DNA synthesis, DNA-bound PCNA could mediate the coupling of MMR with DNA replication.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In vivo PCNA unloading during S-phase largely depends on the Elg1-containing RFC-like complex both in humans and in yeast.
source: Since in vivo PCNA unloading during S-phase largely depends on the Elg1-containing RFC-like complex (Elg1-RLC) both in humans and in yeast (Kubota et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013; Shiomi and Nishitani, 2013; Kubota et al., 2015), the PIP-motif in MutSα may also limit the access of Elg1-RLC to DNA-bound PCNA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kubota et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013; Shiomi and Nishitani, 2013; and Kubota et al., 2015.

claim: The PIP-motif in MutSα may limit the access of Elg1-RLC to DNA-bound PCNA.
source: Since in vivo PCNA unloading during S-phase largely depends on the Elg1-containing RFC-like complex (Elg1-RLC) both in humans and in yeast (Kubota et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013; Shiomi and Nishitani, 2013; Kubota et al., 2015), the PIP-motif in MutSα may also limit the access of Elg1-RLC to DNA-bound PCNA.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known role of Elg1-RLC in PCNA unloading.

claim: The NTR of yeast Msh6 and Msh3 are inter-exchangeable without significant deleterious effects.
source: As seen for MutSα, we predict that MutSβ may inhibit PCNA unloading as well, since the NTR of yeast Msh6 and Msh3 are inter-exchangeable without significant deleterious effects (Shell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shell et al., 2007.

claim: MutSβ may inhibit PCNA unloading.
source: As seen for MutSα, we predict that MutSβ may inhibit PCNA unloading as well, since the NTR of yeast Msh6 and Msh3 are inter-exchangeable without significant deleterious effects (Shell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is predicted based on the similarity between MutSα and MutSβ.

claim: The PIP-deficient MutSα complexes were proficient in repairing a mismatch in the in vitro MMR system.
source: The PIP-deficient MutSα complexes were proficient in repairing a mismatch in our in vitro MMR system (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and similar observations were already reported both in human cell extracts and in a yeast in vitro reconstitution system (Kleczkowska et al., 2001; Iyer et al., 2008; Bowen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: A simple MMR reaction involving a mismatch and a closely-placed strand-discrimination signal would not require retention of PCNA by MutSα.
source: Therefore, a simple MMR reaction involving a mismatch and a closely-placed strand-discrimination signal, either PCNA or a strand discontinuity, would not require retention of PCNA by MutSα.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PIP-deficient MutSα can repair mismatches in simple MMR reactions.

claim: When a stepwise incubation was involved, the PIP motif became important for MMR.
source: However, when a stepwise incubation, which mimics transient arrest of the MMR reaction, was involved, the PIP motif became important for MMR (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Inhibition of PCNA unloading is needed for MMR only under specific situations, e.g. when a strand-discrimination signal is buried within chromatin.
source: We speculate that inhibition of PCNA unloading is needed for MMR only under specific situations, e.g. when a strand-discrimination signal is buried within chromatin.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental observations.

claim: The leading strand seems to have less PCNA than the lagging strand.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2014; Pavlov et al., 2003; and Lujan et al., 2014.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Pavlov et al., 2003 and Lujan et al., 2014.

claim: NPE has been extensively used as a physiological model system that recapitulates various DNA repair reactions coupled with DNA synthesis.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Räschle et al., 2008 and Olivera Harris et al., 2015.

claim: Both 5'-nick directed and 3'-nick directed MMR was dependent on MutL complexes in NPE.
source: In contrast, not only 3'-gap directed but also 5'-gap directed MMR was dependent on MutL complexes in NPE (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: DNA synthesis at the 3'-gap clearly precedes MMR in NPE.
source: Interestingly, DNA synthesis at the 3'-gap clearly precedes MMR (Figure 1F), indicating that strand degradation does not progressively occur from the 3'-terminus of the gap.

claim: Strand degradation does not progressively occur from the 3'-terminus of the gap in NPE.

claim: A nick is suggested to function as a strand signal rather than an entry point for exonucleases in crude extracts of Xenopus eggs.
source: Consistently, a nick is suggested to function as a strand signal rather than an entry point for exonucleases in crude extracts of Xenopus eggs (Varlet et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Varlet et al., 1996.

claim: The PCNA-directed MMR would function in a bidirectional manner.
source: As gap-directed MMR in NPE was bidirectional and preferentially degrades the DNA strand through the shortest path from the gap to the mismatch, we assume that the PCNA-directed MMR would function in the same manner.
evidence: This is assumed based on the similarity to gap-directed MMR.

claim: The strand excision complex presumably built upon a specific face of PCNA would catalyze strand degradation in either direction depending on the relative orientation toward a mismatch.
source: If so, the strand excision complex presumably built upon a specific face of PCNA would catalyze strand degradation in either direction depending on the relative orientation toward a mismatch.
evidence: This is speculated based on the bidirectional nature of MMR.

claim: DNA polymerase δ captures DNA-bound PCNA which is otherwise quickly unloaded by the clamp-unloading activity of RFC.
source: A recent study showed that DNA polymerase δ captures DNA-bound PCNA which is otherwise quickly unloaded by the clamp-unloading activity of RFC (Hedglin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hedglin et al., 2013.

claim: Binding of the PIP motif onto PCNA may physically prevent the engagement of PCNA with RFC.
source: It would be possible that MutSα inhibits PCNA unloading in a similar manner; binding of the PIP motif onto PCNA may physically prevent the engagement of PCNA with RFC.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible mechanism.

claim: MutSα might be able to retain PCNA that is located far from MutSα using its long 'PIP-arm', possibly even over nucleosomes.
source: Although a significant portion of this linker in human MutSα seems to adopt a globular conformation (Iyer et al., 2008), MutSα might be able to retain PCNA that is located far from MutSα using this long 'PIP-arm', possibly even over nucleosomes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structure of MutSα.

claim: Strand removal would initiate when MutLα reaches to PCNA that is retained by the PIP-arm of MutSα.
source: In this scenario, strand removal would initiate when MutLα reaches to PCNA that is retained by the PIP-arm of MutSα.
evidence: This is speculated as part of a proposed mechanism.

claim: Recruitment or retention of PCNA by MutSα around mismatches activates a specific strand removal pathway that is independent of Exo1 in yeast.
source: Interaction between PCNA that is retained by MutSα and MutLα may invoke a specific strand degradation pathway, because a recent study in yeast has suggested that recruitment or retention of PCNA by MutSα around mismatches activates a specific strand removal pathway that is independent of Exo1 (Goellner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goellner et al., 2014.

claim: MutSβ may inhibit PCNA unloading.
source: As seen for MutSα, we predict that MutSβ may inhibit PCNA unloading as well, since the NTR of yeast Msh6 and Msh3 are inter-exchangeable without significant deleterious effects (Shell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is predicted based on the similarity to MutSα.
